name: Watermarking is a provenance signal, not a safety control - it does not moderate, refuse, or prevent anything
symptom: A deployment adds a watermark and reports the content-safety problem as solved. The watermark changes which tokens get sampled; it has no ability to refuse, to filter, or to detect harm at generation time. Harmful content is watermarked exactly as faithfully as benign content.
root_cause: Watermarking operates on the sampling distribution to plant a statistical signal for later verification. It is orthogonal to harm: the mechanism that promotes green tokens has no notion of what the tokens mean. Its output is an attribution claim ('this came from model X') usable only after the fact and only by someone holding the key - which makes it a compliance ARTEFACT rather than a runtime control. The distinction the field itself draws is between safety training (cannot adapt to new attack types, drops performance) and safeguards (external models or filters, of limited help); watermarking is neither.
workaround: If the requirement is 'users must be able to tell AI text from human text', watermarking is a reasonable mechanism and EU AI Act-style marking obligations are what it is for. If the requirement is 'do not serve harmful content', watermarking contributes nothing and you still need in-decode filtering, a guard model, and over-refusal measurement.
notes: The compliance framing is a trap worth naming explicitly: a watermark gives you a defensible answer to 'how do you mark machine-generated content', and it is easy to record that as having addressed content safety. It has not.
